title: Bathla sets off insurance time bomb
full_text:
Crippled western Sydney home builder Bathla Group ran up millions in unpaid bills to NSW insurer icare, which could suffer a cash call as aggrieved homeowners claim on the public purse for defects and non-completion.
Bathla, which builds affordable housing in Sydney, is a ticking time bomb as administrators try to solve the future of the heavily indebted developer. Administrator Teneo says Bathla owes creditors $3.4bn, a figure set to rise as more debts are declared.
Already, lenders are trying to dismember the developer to protect their projects.
Olvera Advisors principal Damien Hodgkinson cautions that its collapse will trigger a $360m call on state insurance agency icare, with a long tail of unfinished homes and defects across thousands of properties weighing on the NSW last resort scheme.
Icare manages the NSW Home Building Compensation Fund, which pays out if something goes awry on a project: either a builder fails and cannot complete work, or major repairs are needed.
“Icare’s exposure is real, will run for years, and is nowhere near the headline debt figure but it is also not insignificant and could run to over $360m,” Mr Hodgkinson said.
“The scheme’s design does most of the work in limiting it and the single biggest limiter is that the people most visibly hurt by this collapse are largely not insured under the scheme at all.” At least 2000 homes were under construction at the time of Bathla’s collapse, many houses and townhouses, alongside apartment projects. These apartment projects will not fall under the HBCF scheme.
Mr Hodgkinson predicted unfinished houses and Bathla’s more than 8000 completed homes would flood NSW’s icare.
A spokesman for the public insurer attempted to minimise concerns related to the Bathla collapse. Documents show icare claimed almost $9.6m in unpaid debts against Bathla.
A spokesman said this reflected workers compensation premiums. Icare also administers workers compensation in NSW, which is mandatory for employers. The spokesman was asked about HBCF arrears, but did not provide an answer.
Icare sought to water down the Olvera Advisors estimate of $360m in claims exposure.
“Icare will continue to engage with the administrator through the voluntary administration process,” a spokesman said. “Icare is unable to provide further comment while the administration process is under way.” Days before Bathla collapsed, the NSW Building Commission fined the group and imposed new licence conditions after discovering the developer had lied about insurance cover on some of its projects. Bathla must pay $20,000 towards insurance for each project at commencement.
But in this case, the commissioner discovered that Bathla was attempting to register insurance as it approached the end of its build on two projects in western Sydney.
Already, Bathla homeowner groups have started to lodge HBCF claims. One homeowner group is aggrieved by unfinished houses, as well as large incomplete common areas planned as parkland but which are little more than muddy paddocks.
Mr Hodgkinson reiterated that icare was “genuinely” exposed to Bathla through claims for non-completion on its house and land packages. These claims are capped at 20 per cent of the contract price.
Further, every homeowner with a Bathla-built property, at three storeys or below, can also draw against the HBCF scheme.
Mr Hodgkinson said icare could face claims of $126m for incomplete homes, assuming average payouts were to hit $140,000. However, at a lower estimate these incomplete claims could be as little as $12m on the insurance scheme.
In addition, Mr Hodgkinson said if up to 8000 Bathla homeowners were to lodge claims for defects, at an average payout of $150,000 in repairs, it could cost up to $240m.
The insurer suffered a $1.7bn loss in 2025 when it paid out $7.6bn in claims, well in excess of its $5.7bn in premiums. However, only $173.8m in HBCF claims were paid. This was from just 749 claims.
While interim financial support has been secured for Bathla, with five lenders to the developer backing a $5m deal to bankroll its operations on a short-term basis, time is running out. Sources close to the lender group say they expect Bathla will require further funding in coming days. If not, it may proceed into liquidation. A spokesman for Teneo declined to comment.
